1) Primary localized cutaneous nodular amyloidosis (most likely) — biopsy shows dermal nodular eosinophilic deposits, scattered plasma cells and strongly Congo red–positive material consistent with AL-type cutaneous amyloid (classic for PLCNA).
2) Cutaneous manifestation of systemic AL (light-chain) amyloidosis — histology can be identical; must be excluded because of possible systemic plasma cell disorder.
3) Secondary/localized (AA-type) cutaneous amyloid from chronic inflammation or prior trauma — less likely given plasma cells and typical nodular appearance, but possible in a localized setting.
4) Cutaneous plasmacytoma with amyloid deposition — solitary plasma-cell tumor of the skin can produce local light-chain amyloid and mimic PLCNA.
5) Cutaneous B‑cell lymphoma with plasmacytic differentiation (e.g., marginal zone lymphoma) producing localized light chains and amyloid — rare but possible.

Rationale summary: The biopsy (abundant eosinophilic/globular dermal material, bright pink collagen bundles, plasma cells, Congo red positive) is diagnostic of amyloid deposition in the lesion; the pattern (solitary indurated plaque with plasma cells) most closely fits primary localized nodular cutaneous amyloidosis but systemic AL and localized plasma‑cell neoplasms must be ruled out.

Recommended next steps (to distinguish localized vs systemic disease and evaluate for an underlying plasma‑cell disorder): serum free light chains (kappa, lambda and ratio), serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation, urine protein electrophoresis with immunofixation (or urine immunofixation), CBC, basic metabolic panel/creatinine, urinalysis (for proteinuria), and hematology referral if any abnormality. Consider bone marrow exam and cardiac evaluation (ECG/echo) if labs suggest systemic involvement.
